Review by PTAbro 27

Leave it to Kurosawa to make an hour of listing evidence and clues exciting.

High and Low is tight, tense, and engaging, but what makes it so great for me is that Kurosawa (based on the book King's Ransom by Ed McBain) uses an almost Dante-like structuring of the three points of view by which this story is told. Each act is a discrete and self-contained plot with its own beginning, middle, and end, which make High and Low more of a crime anthology than an epic. Still, all the main characters appear (physically or vocally) in all three stories, tying them together and leaving room for an epilogue which unites the circuitous narrative. Review by Josh Lewis 7

"That house gets on your nerves. [It's] as if it's looking down at us."

Akira Kurosawa was accused a number of times throughout his career of being one of the few Japanese filmmakers to be so popular and celebrated on the international stage because of how often he adapted western works and adopted western influences in his style to tell them. Yet despite High and Low’s premise being sourced from an American kidnapping thriller/police procedural novel by Ed McBain and certainly realizing stretches of it it in a precise, noir-ishly stylized fashion, it remains one of Kurosawa’s sharpest and most specific interrogations of post-war Japanese society, those who benefitted from the modern consumerist economic boom it experienced in those years…

Review by Sean Baker 21

Had the pleasure of watching this film for the first time on 35mm thanks to The Cinematheque in Vancouver. It was the first film in the series High Art Films Made from Pop Art Sources curated by Donald Brackett. Brackett intro'd the film.

Great film by a great master. Incredibly tight Tohoscope framing which should be studied for how to frame groups of characters in a 2.35 frame.

trivia: Pulp Fiction's "Swing Dance Scene" was inspired by the incredible real time dance scene in the last act of High and Low.

Watched on 35mm at Vancouver's Cinematheque

Review by Will Menaker 7

A masterpiece of Noir/police procedural that spares not a single detail. This movie is part of a lineage of painstaking procedurals about the investigation of a crime that become a forensic examination of the society in which they occur. It goes M--->High and Low--->The Boston Strangler--->Memories of Murder--->Zodiac.

The first 50 minutes of this takes places entirely in a guy's living room and just with how he composes people in space--entering a room, getting up, sitting down--Kurosawa shows you absolutely everything you need to know about feel about the action thats taking place. Masterclass, tears in my eyes.

Review by Darren Carver-Balsiger 25

Weirdly enough, the world of High and Low contains fundamentally good people. There is an evil criminal and heartless businessmen, but when things get tough, the people do the right thing. High and Low is rarely subtle in its class allusions, but it gives us sympathy for the wealthy lead, even after painting him callously when we realise the monetary value he initially places on the lives of different children. This is a film of affluence and poverty, of hierarchical systems within society (like the poor man tough on his child but meek when facing his boss). If a rich man exists, there must exist those who are poorer.

This was the last of 14 Mifune films I watched to prepare for an episode dedicated to the actor roughly one month into lockdown in 2020. I don't know why I stopped there, but it's notable. It's the second-to-last collaboration he made with Kurosawa, and the one that seems to confront their station in life most plainly: two upper-middle class men who rose in post-war Japan to become iconic symbols of artistic innovation and professional efficiency.
